An Investor Letter From Cathie Wood

An Investor Letter From Cathie Wood

September 22, 2026
41 min read

By: Cathie Wood

Chief Executive Officer,

Chief Investment Officer

Cathie founded ARK to focus solely on investing in disruptive innovation while adding new dimensions to research. Through an open research approach, Cathie believes ARK can identify large-scale investment opportunities resulting from technological innovations.

Contributors: Dan White, CFA, Portfolio Manager, and Dzhan Yusnyu, Associate Portfolio ManagerIntroductionNow in the financial services sector for more than 40 years, I am struck that most trends in the US economy are “back to the future,” except interest rates. The secular decline in interest rates started from 15-20% in the early eighties and ended at 0.5-2% during the COVID-related crash in 2020. Now, interest rates are hitting “higher highs” for the first time in more than 40 years; yet, the US equity market has been climbing toward all-time highs, puzzling many concerned investors.In this paper, we share our thoughts on the technology revolution that could push real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth and interest rates higher while inflation falls and the yield curve inverts. Not since the Industrial Revolution have we witnessed this confluence of economic indicators.Interest Rates In The Context Of 200+ Years Of HistoryInterest rates declined from 1981 through 2021, a trend that broke decisively in 2022 and has unnerved investors. In the context of 230 years of history, however, the anomaly was the sharp rise and fall of interest rates over the sixty years ending in 2021, as shown in green in the chart below. Starting in the sixties, the US government began supporting both “guns and butter”—aka the Vietnam War and the Great Society—and then closed the gold window in 1971 so that monetary policy could accommodate those programs. The result was double digit inflation and interest rates. In the early eighties, the Reagan Administration and the Volcker Federal Reserve (Fed) began to tackle them, setting in motion the move toward near zero inflation and interest rates forty years later.Note: Pre-1857 recessions are not officially dated by NBER and are not shaded. Shaded areas represent recessions. Data are US long-term nominal sovereign yield, 1790-1961; Federal Reserve Board via FRED, series GS10 is10-Year Treasury constant-maturity yield, annual average, 1962-2026; 2026 is year-to-date through July. Source: ARK Investment Management LLC, 2026, based on data from Schmelzing 2020 and Federal Reserve Board via FRED.1 For informational purposes only and should not be considered investment advice or a recommendation to buy, sell, or hold any particular security.Long-term interest rates today are at the lower end of the range in place from the early 1800s through the Industrial Revolution until the Great Depression in the 1930s. According to our research, the technology revolution now underway should have a much more powerful impact on the global economy than did the Industrial Revolution, suggesting that interest rates should move higher on average than the ~3-6% range in place during the 130 years prior to the Great Depression. The equity market seems to be adjusting to this higher rate regime, perhaps because real yields, not inflation, are behind the recent increase in long yields.Back To The Future: Another Golden Age For Equities?In the eighties and nineties, the equity market climbed a “wall of worry”—inflation, interest rates, government deficits and debt, trade quotas, the Gulf wars, the savings and loan crisis, and a technology transition from mainframes and landlines to PCs and wireless. In hindsight, the wall of worry led to the most durable equity bull market since the Roaring Twenties.Today, uncannily, the headlines are the same: inflation, interest rates, government deficits and debt, trade tariffs, the Russia and Iran wars, the private credit debacle, and a technology revolution catalyzed by AI. Adding to those concerns is fear that AI hype is creating another technology bubble, especially because the elder statesmen and women in the industry today were in the early years of their careers back then: “Been there, done that, never again” is influencing the current zeitgeist.In this update, we present evidence supporting our forecast that:Inflation is on the verge of breaking down;Real GDP growth is likely to accelerate significantly above the 2-3% range in place globally since the Industrial Revolution;The yield curve is likely to invert without causing a recession, much like during the Industrial Revolution;Short-term interest rates are likely to turn back up in tandem with nominal GDP growth, putting at risk companies on the wrong side of change, especially those highly leveraged with floating rate debt.Inflation Is On The Verge Of Breaking DownInflation OverviewSince the COVID-related boom/bust, again much like in the eighties and nineties, the equity market has been grappling with fears that inflation will goad the US Federal Reserve (Fed) into a more hawkish policy stance. In our view, if and when the current bout of war-related oil price hikes subsides, the higher probability is that inflation will surprise on the low side of expectations, perhaps much lower, thanks to Fed Chair Warsh-led monetary discipline, a significant drop in oil prices, and waves of deflation caused by this technology revolution.Based on our understanding of his theoretical framework for monetary policy and the five task forces he has commissioned, Warsh seems committed to the “back-to-the-future” policies of Fed Chairman Volcker. Maniacally focused on the impact of money growth on inflation, Volcker pushed headline Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation down from 11.6% on a year-over-year basis at its peak in March 1980 to 1.6% during his term, as shown in green below, and core PCE inflation—excluding food and energy—down from 9.8% to 2.8%.Echoing Volcker, Warsh has focused three of the five task forces he commissioned on inflation measures, inflation frameworks, and productivity’s impact on inflation. Importantly, he seems open to monitoring real-time private measures of inflation, some of which have diverged considerably from government measures. As measured by the government’s headline and core PCE deflators, Warsh’s preferred government measures, inflation has hovered in the 2% to 4% range for the past three years, ending well above the Fed’s target at 3.7% and 3.3%, respectively, in July, as shown below. In our view, the Iran War is exacerbating the Russia/Ukraine supply side shock that began in 2023 but, the longer it lasts, the greater drop in oil prices occur when peace breaks out, as discussed later in this piece.Source: ARK Investment Management LLC, 2026, based on data from Bureau of Economic Analysis via FRED as of August 28, 2026.2 For informational purposes only and should not be considered investment advice or a recommendation to buy, sell, or hold any particular security.As measured by Truflation, headline and core PCE inflation have decelerated from ~9.5% and ~7.1% at their respective peaks after COVID to 2.5% and 2.1%, as shown below. Back-tested since 2010 and launched in December 2021, Truflation updates real-time price inflation across more than 16 million consumer goods and services daily. (Please see the Appendix for a comparison of the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) and Truflation measures of inflation.) According to Truflation, the Fed is not 170 and 130 basis points3 away from its 2% goal, but within 50 basis points as measured by headline PCE Truflation, and 10 basis points as measured by core PCE Truflation, as shown below.  Source: ARK Investment Management LLC, 2026, based on data from Truflation as of September 18, 2026.4 For informational purposes only and should not be considered investment advice or a recommendation to buy, sell, or hold any particular security.Inflation: Gold And The DollarInterestingly, this year the gold price hit an intraday all-time-high of $5,595 per ounce on January 29, 2026, the day before President Trump publicly nominated Kevin Warsh as Fed Chairman. During Chairman Volcker’s term, the gold price peaked at ~$850 per ounce in January 1980 and dropped more than 50% to ~$300 per ounce in June 1982.In the next two years, we would not be surprised to see the gold price decline as tax cuts, deregulation, and the technology revolution boost both productivity growth and the returns on invested capital in the US relative to those in the rest of the world. As in the eighties, the dollar could become “as good as gold,” driving inflation to levels much lower than most economists and policymakers now expect.Contrary to the current narrative, the dollar has not been weak relative to the currencies of our trade partners. Indeed, since the Global Financial Crisis5 (“GFC”), the U.S. Dollar Index (DXY) has appreciated more than 35%6 relative to six of our larger trading partners and is hovering at the average around which it has traded since 1970, as shown below.Note: Bloomberg (DXY Index) is a fixed-weight geometric average against six currencies (EUR, JPY, GBP, CAD, SEK, CHF) whose weights have been unchanged since 1973, apart from the euro’s 1999 replacement of legacy European currencies; it is not a trade-weighted index. 2026 calculations by ARK Investment Management LLC. Recessions per National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER). 2023. 'US Business Cycle Expansions and Contractions." Source: ARK Investment Management LLC, 2026, based on data from Bloomberg (DXY Index).7 For informational purposes only and should not be considered investment advice or a recommendation to buy, sell, or hold any particular security.Perhaps more important, as measured against the 26 countries in the Fed’s Broad Index, the dollar is up 36%8 since the GFC and is now 44% above its long-term average, as shown below. Explaining the difference between the two trade-weighted dollar averages are the number of countries and their trade weights: surprisingly, in the more heavily traded DXY, trade weights have not changed in more than 50 years, whereas the Fed updates the weights in its Broad Index annually.Source: ARK Investment Management LLC, 2026, based on data from US Federal Reserve Board via FRED.9 For informational purposes only and should not be considered investment advice or a recommendation to buy, sell, or hold any particular security.In other words, contrary to the prevailing narrative, the dollar has not been weak relative to other currencies; nor do we believe it will be weak. Indeed, we would not be surprised to see significant appreciation during the next few years, much like in the early eighties, for the same reasons: sound monetary policy, business-friendly fiscal policies, and a technology revolution favoring returns on invested capital in the US relative to the rest of the world.That said, unlike in the eighties and nineties, the purchasing power of the dollar in terms of gold has collapsed. Indeed, since the bottom of the tech and telecom bust in 2003,10 the dollar has lost 92% of its purchasing power, slightly more than the 90% lost in the ten years11 after the US closed the gold window in 1971, as shown below. With stability as the Fed’s “North Star,” we believe Fed Chairman Warsh is likely to emulate Chairmen Volcker and Greenspan, who seemed to use the gold price as one of their primary monetary policy guides, as illustrated in green by its behavior during their respective terms in the chart below. We would not be surprised to see the gold price decline during Fed Chairman Warsh’s term.Source: ARK Investment Management LLC, 2026, based on data from Macrobond.12 For informational purposes only and should not be considered investment advice or a recommendation to buy, sell, or hold any particular security.Deflation: Oil PricesEnergy and energy-related price increases have been camouflaging price declines elsewhere in the consumer market basket. As measured by Truflation, gasoline and other energy goods prices are up ~33% year-over-year, which, based on its 2.0% weight in the PCE, has contributed 0.7 percentage points to the latest 2.5% headline Truflation PCE inflation rate as of September 18, 2026.In our view, oil prices are on the threshold of a significant decline. Recently, the International Energy Agency (IEA) issued revised projections that global oil production will drop 5.7 million barrels per day (mbd) to 100.7 mbd and that global oil demand will drop 2.5 mbd. Clearly, the surge in prices in response to the Iran War has caused both supply bottlenecks and demand destruction. Electric vehicles have been among the prime beneficiaries.Meanwhile, with the help of US oil companies, oil production is beginning to ramp in countries with spare capacity, like Venezuela, Libya, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), the latter having dropped out of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) in May and Venezuela now threatening to do the same. An important question is whether Saudi Arabia—now with ~3.9 mbd of excess capacity—will continue to serve as OPEC’s swing producer as the Strait of Hormuz reopens.In 1986, after an increasing number of OPEC members had been cheating on their quotas, Saudi Arabia reacted by increasing production dramatically to remind the cartel who was in control: oil prices dropped ~60%, from ~$23 to ~$9 per barrel. Measured in today’s dollars, that drop would have been from ~$87 to ~$35 per barrel. Today, Iraq, Nigeria, and Kazakhstan are cheating on their quotas and, according to Bloomberg, after dropping out of OPEC in May, the UAE increased its production 78% from ~2.3 mbd in March to a record ~4.1mbd in June, and probably more since then. As a result, despite the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, the response in oil prices has been relatively muted. During the next few years, we would not be surprised to see the oil price drop back toward ~$30-35 per barrel which, apart from the COVID-related crash, is the low end of the wide trading range in place since 2000, as shown below.Source: ARK Investment Management LLC, 2026, based on data from Bloomberg and Macrobond.13 For informational purposes only and should not be considered investment advice or a recommendation to buy, sell, or hold any particular security.Based on its serious and successful focus on technologically enabled innovation during the past five to ten years, perhaps the UAE—led by Abu Dhabi—believes that natural gas, nuclear power, hydropower, wind/solar and battery technology will power electric robotaxis, autonomous trucks, drones, flying taxis, and robots in this technology revolution. In other words, transportation—accounting for ~57% of global oil demand14—may be transitioning to the grid, suggesting that the value of oil reserves may have peaked secularly when the price hit ~$145 per barrel in 2008. With the oil price up 50-60% from ~$60 earlier this year to $90-100 as of September 17,15 the time to maximize production could be now. Based on the pent-up supply built up behind the Strait of Hormuz, oil prices could drop precipitously once peace breaks out and the Strait opens.Deflation: TechnologyDeflation can be good news. A significant drop in oil prices would be the equivalent of a tax cut for most consumers and businesses. Likewise, when technology companies pass along their cost declines, consumers enjoy breakthrough products and services that increase their quality of life, and businesses benefit from both stronger growth and higher margins, if they are on the right side of change.Based on seeds planted in the 20 years that ended in the tech and telecom bust, five major innovation platforms—AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain technology, and multiomics sequencing—have been germinating for the last 20-25 years. They involve 15 technologies that are mature enough now to impact economic growth and inflation meaningfully.Given the cloud’s debut in 2006 and the significant breakthroughs in artificial intelligence—deep learning in 2012, transformer architecture in 2017, and large language models in 2018—the cost of the AI inference that powers ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok to complete tasks is dropping 99%+ per year, as shown below. Meanwhile, the cost to sequence one whole human genome has collapsed from $2.7 billion in 2003 to less than $100, also shown below, and should continue to drop 40% for every cumulative doubling in the number of whole human genomes sequenced. Note how much more quickly costs are falling today!Source: ARK Investment Management LLC, 2026, based on data from National Human Genome Research Institute 2022, ARK Investment Management LLC 2020, a16z 2024, Epoch AI 2025, and NBER 2023.16 For informational purposes only and should not be considered investment advice or a recommendation to buy, sell, or hold any particular security.In 2025, as AI inference costs dropped more than 99% and the demand for AI inference tokens soared an astonishing 25-fold, the frontier model providers generated revenue growth the likes of which we have not seen at any other time in history. From December through July, Anthropic’s annualized revenue run rate (ARR) soared more than seven-fold, from $9 billion to $65 billion and, according to our estimates, could top $100 billion while generating much higher-than-expected profitability by year-end. In other words, Anthropic increased its revenue over seven months by more than Salesforce did in 25 years. No AI “hype” in those numbers!Good deflation is causing an explosion in unit and revenue growth rates that are beginning to move macroeconomic needles. As a result, the US economy has powered through rising rates, inverted yield curves, tariffs, government shutdowns, and wars, and it should continue to generate surprisingly high growth rates in the years ahead, as discussed below.Real GDP Growth Is Likely To Accelerate Significantly Above The 2 To 3% Range In Place Globally Since The Industrial RevolutionReal GDP Growth, Productivity, And Interest RatesIf our research is pointing us in the right direction, back to the last technology revolution in the 50 years that ended in the Roaring Twenties, real GDP growth is likely to accelerate well above 3%, the rate in place since the Industrial Revolution, to 7%+, as shown below. At the same time, inflation is likely to drop well below the Fed’s targeted 2%, and the yield curve could invert as short rates follow nominal activity while long rates take more cues from inflation in the -2% to +2% range. In other words, short rates could rise to 6-8% in tandem with nominal GDP growth while long rates approach 5-6%.From 1500 to 1900, years of limited innovation until the Industrial Revolution, real GDP growth averaged 0.6% per year. In the following 125 years, the step function in real growth was five-fold to 3% at an annual rate, as shown below in a chart authored by Brett Winton, ARK’s Chief Futurist. Three technologically enabled innovation platforms drove the Industrial Revolution: electricity, telephone, and the internal combustion engine. Powered by five major platforms, the current technology revolution is likely to dwarf the Industrial Revolution, suggesting that 7% growth—only a ~2.5-fold increase—could be a conservative estimate for the next five years. Indeed, Elon Musk, the inventor of our time, would not be surprised to see real GDP grow 20 to 30% in our time!17Source: ARK Investment Management LLC, 2026, based on data from Winton 2026, Kremer 1993, and DeLong 1998.18 For informational purposes only and should not be considered investment advice or a recommendation to buy, sell, or hold any particular security. Forecasts are inherently limited and cannot be relied upon.Technology-driven productivity is likely to be the prime mover behind 7%+ real GDP growth. Based on a four-year moving average, productivity growth in the eighties and nineties accelerated from ~0% to ~3.5%, a range that should pale in comparison to that likely during the next five to ten years. We would not be surprised to see sustainable productivity gains in the 5-6% range.Source: ARK Investment Management LLC, 2026, based on data from U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.19 For informational purposes only and should not be considered investment advice or a recommendation to buy, sell, or hold any particular security. Forecasts are inherently limited and cannot be relied upon.Productivity gains should give company management teams on the right side of change some or all the following options: bolstering margins, reinvesting in research and development (R&D) and capital spending, increasing compensation, and/or lowering prices. Given the massive returns on invested capital associated with this technology revolution, most companies are likely to invest aggressively in R&D and capital spending. To compete more aggressively with China, US companies also might lower prices. To rebalance its economy toward consumption, Chinese companies might favor higher compensation. Rebalancing the competitive dynamics between China and the US is an interesting win-win possibility in a rational geopolitical environment.The Yield Curve Is Likely To Invert Without Causing A Recession, Much Like During The Industrial RevolutionYield CurveDuring the 50 years that ended during the Roaring Twenties in 1929, the yield curve was inverted more than 60% of the time, on average by slightly more than 100 bps, as shown below. Short rates averaged 4.8%, tracking 4.8% nominal GDP growth—3.7% real growth and 1.1% inflation—while long rates averaged 3.8%,20 the latter discounting the deflationary undercurrents that new technologies were spawning.Unlike the last hundred years, positively sloped yield curves were rare during the Industrial Revolution, as shown below. Prior to the creation of the Federal Reserve in 1913, the economy was much more prone to downturns than it is today, as depicted by the shaded areas in the chart below. Consistent with the analyses of NBER researcher Michael D. Bordo and collaborators,21 short rates rose with real growth, while long rates lagged in response to lower inflation, a combination that accompanied a sustained boom in equity markets.Source: ARK Investment Management LLC, 2026, based on data from PK DQYDJ.com.22 For informational purposes only and should not be considered investment advice or a recommendation to buy, sell, or hold any particular security.Innovation platforms today are evolving at a rate faster than those in the late 1800’s. Perhaps contributing to some confusion, the government still reports economic statistics designed in and for the industrial age as gauges of activity in the digital age. As a result, they probably are understating real growth and productivity, and overstating inflation. Combined with tax reform and deregulation in both the US and China, the five technologically enabled platforms could unleash tsunamis of innovation that will change the way the world works, creating a deflationary boom rivaling that which led to the Roaring Twenties early in the twentieth century. In that environment, an inversion of the yield curve would be exceedingly good news for the equity markets.Today, the yield curve is picking up on this “back to the future” theme. Since the tech and telecom bust roughly 25 years ago, it has been peaking at lower levels with each cycle, as shown below. In our view, it is likely to return to negative territory, where it was on balance prior to the Roaring Twenties, without signaling an imminent recession. The only time since 1929 that the yield curve flirted with inversion without signaling a recession was during a credit crunch in 1966. From 2022 to 2024, the economy weathered an inverted yield curve without falling into a recession, perhaps reaffirming that economic conditions today are more consistent with the Industrial Revolution than those after the Great Depression.Note: Macrobond (Series "United States, Government Benchmarks, Federal Reserve, 10 Year-2 Year") and cross-referenced against Bloomberg (USGG10YR Index, USGG2YR Index; spread consistent with Bloomberg USYC2Y10 Index). Recessions per National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) 2023. Gray shaded areas represent recessions as denoted by the NBER. Source: ARK Investment Management LLC, 2026, based on data from Macrobond.23 For informational purposes only and should not be considered investment advice or a recommendation to buy, sell, or hold any particular security.Short-Term Interest Rates Are Likely To Turn Back Up In Tandem With Nominal GDP Growth, Putting At Risk Companies On The Wrong Side Of Change, Especially Those Highly Leveraged With Floating Rate Debt.Spoilers: Bankruptcies Amid Unsustainable Government Debt?If this deflationary technology revolution continues to gather momentum, disrupting the traditional world order in ways that businesses and investors do not anticipate, broad-based bankruptcies could pose serious counterparty risks throughout the system—a good reason for potential insurance policies like gold and bitcoin.The demand for credit to fund the convergence of the physical and digital worlds—autonomous transportation, autonomous delivery, and terrestrial/orbital data centers—is exploding and could continue to push GDP growth and interest rates higher than most economists would expect in a world trending toward price deflation. Funded primarily by floating rate debt, ~$16 trillion24 in private equity and private credit could fall victim to this disruption. Debt and equity tied to the old-world order could become toxic. SaaS-pocalypse25 may have been just the beginning.Not to be outdone is excessive Federal government debt at $40 trillion, just shy of 125% of GDP, that is dwarfing private equity and private debt at little more than 50% of GDP. If short rates were to increase 200 basis points (2%), the Federal government’s debt service would increase by $800 billion, almost the size of the US defense budget, while the private equity and credit funds populated by companies in harm’s way would have to cough up ~$300 billion somewhere, a serious issue if their portfolio companies begin to falter or unravel.That said, we believe that comparing a balance sheet metric—debt—to an income statement metric—GDP—is somewhat misleading for companies and countries in growth, super-growth, and productivity mode. Instead, debt to equity, the latter benefiting from rising revenues, productivity, and profitability, is more relevant, in our view. Although the US Federal Debt-to-GDP is near an all-time high, US Federal Debt to US Equity is near an all-time low, as shown below. With enough growth, the US government could repeat the success it enjoyed during the internet revolution and generate its first surplus in 30 years during the next five to ten years.Note: Gray shaded areas represent recessions as denoted by the NBER. Source: ARK Investment Management LLC, 2026, based on data from Macrobond.26 For informational purposes only and should not be considered investment advice or a recommendation to buy, sell, or hold any particular security.ConclusionARK’s research on technologically enabled innovation is informing our macroeconomic forecast: a significant acceleration in the growth rates of productivity and real GDP, much lower than expected inflation—if not deflation—and higher interest rates, but inverted yield curves.If correct, this outlook should be more constructive for equities than for fixed income, suggesting that asset allocators may want to consider shifting “balanced portfolios” from the successful formula that worked from 1981 to 2021—60% equities and 40% fixed income—toward a higher proportion of equities, and perhaps bitcoin, at the expense of fixed income.In our view, bottom line, get on the right side of change and ride this innovation super cycle!AppendixTruflation (with BLS weights/categories) versus BEA year-over-year as of July 2026. ARK and its clients as well as its related persons may (but do not necessarily) have financial interests in securities or issuers that are discussed.Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the total monetary or market value of all the finished goods and services produced within a country’s borders in a specific time period. Nominal GDP is a measure of economic output that uses current prices and does not adjust for inflation. Real GDP is an economic metric that is used to describe the economic output of a country within a specific year. It reflects the value of all goods and services produced while factoring inflation into its calculation.Yield Curve is a graphical representation of the interest rates on debt for a range of maturities. It shows the yield an investor is expecting to earn if they lend their money for a given period of time. An inverted curve appears when long-term yields fall below short-term yields. An inverted yield curve occurs due to the perception of long-term investors that interest rates will decline in the future.A real yield is the interest rate an investor earns on a bond or other fixed-income investment after accounting for inflation, reflecting the actual increase in purchasing power over time.Headline PCE reflects the total change in prices for all goods and services consumed by households, including food, energy, housing, healthcare, transportation, and other items. It captures the immediate cost-of-living pressures that consumers face daily, making it a direct measure of how expensive life has become in the short term. Core PCE, on the other hand, excludes food and energy prices, which are highly volatile due to factors like weather, geopolitical events, and supply disruptions. By removing these categories, core PCE provides a clearer view of persistent, underlying inflation trends that are more relevant for long-term economic planning and monetary policy.©2026, ARK Investment Management LLC.
